episodes.place: Jerusalem; no precise neighborhood/refuge location substantiated here
episodes.selectedClaim: Roman legions destroyed the Jerusalem Temple after the revolt.

references.reference: Josephus, Jewish War VI.4-5, especially §§4-5; VI.10 for capture/fall
references.directlyConsulted: Opened and read English Whiston translation paragraphs on fire, dates, Titus's response, and capture: page lines 175-181 and 329-332. It says the Temple fire began on the tenth of Lous/Ab in Josephus's chronology and Jerusalem was taken on eighth of Gorpiaeus/Elul.
references.supports: Josephus narrates the Roman capture and destruction of Jerusalem/Temple in 70 CE; his narrative gives two different calendrical dates for fire and capture.
references.limits: Translation and editorial apparatus are Whiston; Greek critical text not checked. Josephus was a participant and wrote under Flavian patronage. His narrative itself varies about the fire's origin/culpability. It does not authenticate his theological claims or provide a neutral chain of command.

episodes.conflictsAndGeography: Use 70 CE. Keep date-of-fire distinct from date-of-city-capture; do not treat a modern Temple Mount location pin as a precise 70 CE scene footprint.

imageCandidates.author: Daniel Ventura
imageCandidates.directlyConsulted: Commons file page, description, author and license lines 119-147. Description says the model represents Jerusalem c.66 CE, four years before destruction, based on Michael Avi-Yonah's interpretation of Josephus.
imageCandidates.limitations: Modern model and modern scholarly reconstruction, not primary archaeological image; c.66 representation is close context but not an eyewitness depiction of the 70 siege. Any adaptation must comply with attribution/share-alike.

imageCandidates.author: Chesdovi
imageCandidates.directlyConsulted: Commons file page lines 113-122: photo of Israel Museum Temple Mount model; uploader releases photo to public domain.
imageCandidates.limitations: The frame shows a modern model, not a surviving ancient structure; image's short caption gives no modeled date or interpretation. Candidate only.

episodes.date: c.70-80 CE (selected date is not independently pinned by direct evidence)
episodes.place: Yavneh/Jamnia (modern Yavne); exact ancient school site not established by sources read
episodes.selectedClaim: Yohanan ben Zakkai and scholars are associated with rabbinic activity at Yavneh.

references.reference: Center for Online Judaic Studies, 'Tannaitic Literature (circa 70-3rd century CE)', excerpt, lines 22-30; excerpt reproduces/derives from Lawrence H. Schiffman, From Text to Tradition
references.directlyConsulted: Read the accessible excerpt. It associates tannaitic activity after Temple destruction with Yavneh, Usha, Beth Shearim and Sepphoris; says transmission involved divergent opinions. It calls Akiva's link to Yavneh later tradition and says exact responsibility cannot be determined.
references.supports: Post-70 tannaitic transmission is associated in modern synthesis with multiple centers including Yavneh.
references.limits: The consulted excerpt does not directly establish a dated 70-80 school scene or the named Yohanan ben Zakkai claim. The underlying rabbinic texts were not opened for this audit. It does not support a single formal academy's exact founding.

references.directlyConsulted: Page retrieval returned an internal error in this audit; no page text verified here.
references.supports: Nothing independently assessed from this URL in this pass.
references.limits: Do not represent as directly checked in this audit.

episodes.conflictsAndGeography: Treat Yavneh as a place associated with post-Temple rabbinic activity in later source traditions and modern synthesis. A precise 70-80 founding date, school building, formal institutional continuity, or single 'Council of Jamnia' is not supported by the passage read.

episodes.date: c.80-100 CE (broadly illustrative; no exact start date established)
episodes.place: Yavneh and other tannaitic centers; source does not document a single geographic network map
episodes.selectedClaim: Legal traditions and scholarly activity sustained Jewish life after the loss of the Temple.

references.directlyConsulted: Read excerpt lines 20 and 22-32. It describes the Mishnah as compiled from discrete attributed statements; post-Temple activity at Yavneh, Usha, Beth Shearim and Sepphoris; transmission of divergent views; and later redaction with uncertain timing.
references.supports: A process of preserving, transmitting, organizing and redacting legal traditions after 70, over more than one center and period.
references.limits: This is a modern excerpt/synthesis rather than the complete book or contemporaneous documentation. It does not prove a coordinated 'network' operating exactly c.80-100 or an unbroken institutional organization.

episodes.conflictsAndGeography: Avoid locating one unified academy at Yavneh for the whole period. The consulted synthesis names several centers and stresses uncertainty about when redaction began.

episodes.date: c.90-100 CE in the selection; the cited rabbinic traditions are later and do not date a specific Yavneh debate to this interval
episodes.place: Yavneh as the episode's selected setting; the primary passage does not itself locate the debate at Yavneh
episodes.selectedClaim: Rabbinic traditions preserve disagreements about Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs.

references.reference: Mishnah Yadayim 3:5, English and Hebrew text, PDF pp.16-17 (printed locators around lines 241-275)
references.directlyConsulted: Read the displayed passage. It records named positions attributed to Rabbi Yehudah, Yosei, Shimon, Shimon ben Azzai and Akiva on whether Song of Songs/Ecclesiastes 'defile the hands'.
references.supports: The received Mishnah text represents disagreements and a tradition that both books' status was discussed; Akiva's praise of Song of Songs is part of that later textual tradition.
references.limits: This source is a modern PDF reproduction/translation of the Mishnah, not an early manuscript or contemporaneous transcript. The saying about 72 elders is internal attributed tradition, not independent proof of a historical council. It does not place a dated debate at Yavneh, establish closure of the canon, or prove the historical accuracy of later attributions.

references.reference: Mariusz Rosik, 'The Christian Question in Jamnia Academy at the End of the 1st Century AD?'; article landing page abstract
references.directlyConsulted: Read title, abstract and bibliography on the journal page (lines 14-38 and 92-123); full article text was not opened/read. Abstract challenges the synod/canon/Septuagint claims, but advances its own conclusion about Christians being excluded.
references.supports: The cited scholarship explicitly treats 'Council of Jamnia' claims as contested and identifies canon-setting as part of a debated historiographical construction.
references.limits: Only abstract and bibliography were read; do not cite it as if the full article's argument was evaluated. The abstract's conclusion about exclusion is not independently established by this audit.

episodes.conflictsAndGeography: The selected date/location is not supported by Mishnah Yadayim 3:5. Rabbinic discussion of scriptural status is later textual evidence; the passage cannot establish a one-time Jamnia synod or a settled canon-making event at Yavneh.

episodes.date: 96 CE (Nerva's reign; coin issue date and exact reform timing should be confirmed in numismatic catalog)
episodes.place: Rome is directly represented by Suetonius's court anecdote; selection's Rome-Ostia pairing is not evidenced by that anecdote
episodes.selectedClaim: Nerva advertised removal of abuses in the Jewish tax; Suetonius describes intrusive enforcement under Domitian.

references.reference: Suetonius, Domitian 12.2, J.C. Rolfe translation, quoted by Posen Library; entry notes Loeb vol. II (1914), pp.365-367
references.directlyConsulted: Read the quoted passage and its source credit, Posen lines 32-49. Suetonius claims Domitian's fiscus Judaicus was rigorously enforced and recounts a public examination of a 90-year-old man's circumcision; Suetonius says he witnessed it in youth.
references.supports: A literary report that Domitian's tax enforcement could be intrusive, and that Suetonius presents himself as an eyewitness to one examination.
references.limits: Suetonius is a retrospective biographer; the episode gives no specific date or evidence of Ostia. It does not quantify incidence or prove uniform policy across provinces.

references.reference: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, Münzkabinett, Nerva coin catalog record; obverse/reverse legend and catalog commentary
references.directlyConsulted: Read catalog fields 60-68: reverse legend FISCI IVDAICI CALVMNIA SVBLATA; catalog interprets it as withdrawal of hardships in collection of the special tax under Nerva, with references RIC II no.82 and numismatic literature.
references.supports: A coin's public message under Nerva advertised 'calumny/abuse of the fiscus Judaicus removed'; supports a claim of advertised correction, not abolition of the tax.
references.limits: The record did not expose an exact issue year beyond Nerva reign context in text inspected; catalogue interpretation is secondary. Need item-level dating/citation before assigning exact 96 issue date. It says correction of harsh collection, not abolishment.

episodes.conflictsAndGeography: The selected place is Rome-Ostia but the ancient passage is a hearing at Rome. No consulted evidence supports an Ostia archive/scene. Claudius 25 belongs to ca.49 CE and is not evidence for this 90-110 event. Nerva's coin legend refers to removal of calumnia/abuse, not repeal of tax.

episodes.date: c.100-135 CE; Akiva's career broadly placed c.80-132 by consulted synthesis; death/martyrdom chronology remains traditional and contested
episodes.place: Lod is the selected episode setting; source consulted does not document this specific teaching activity in Lod
episodes.selectedClaim: Rabbi Akiva and colleagues transmitted tannaitic legal and liturgical traditions.

references.directlyConsulted: Read passage identifying Akiva's Yavneh floruit as c.80-132, with attribution to later tradition/modern scholars, uncertainty about his role in systematization, and post-132 work at Usha.
references.supports: Legal treatises and organizational traditions were developing in Akiva's broadly assigned lifetime; Akiva is traditionally associated with Yavneh.
references.limits: Modern synthesis; no contemporary biography or direct source for a Lod teaching scene, particular escort, liturgical event, or death date. It explicitly says exact responsibility cannot be determined.

episodes.conflictsAndGeography: Reject c.150-180 activity for Akiva as anachronistic under the selected chronology. Keep Lod as local fictional staging only unless a separate source supports it; do not claim the COJS excerpt places Akiva there.

episodes.date: 115-117 CE (revolt episode broadly dated to Trajan's final eastern campaigns)
episodes.place: Cyrene/Cyrenaica; exact local battle/refuge site not supplied by sources consulted
episodes.selectedClaim: Diaspora revolts affected Cyrenaica, Egypt and Cyprus during Trajan's war.

references.reference: Cassius Dio, Roman History 68.32.1-3, Cary translation of the surviving epitome
references.directlyConsulted: Read lines 152-155. Dio places revolt under Andreas in Cyrene, reports analogous uprisings in Egypt and Cyprus under Artemion, and says Lusius was among those who subdued them.
references.supports: Ancient literary evidence for unrest in Cyrene, Egypt and Cyprus during Trajan's eastern wars and Roman suppression.
references.limits: Dio's text survives through later epitome/transmission; this passage's extravagant atrocity allegations and huge casualty numbers are not independently corroborated by this source and should not be repeated as facts. Does not provide a map footprint or prove one unified command across all regions.

references.reference: Posen Library entry and source excerpt, Cassius Dio 68.32.1-3 (Loeb citation listed by entry)
references.directlyConsulted: Read opened page source/description; page search result exposes source identification and region; some page content was not accessible in line view. Primary Dio passage was separately read at Chicago above.
references.supports: Useful scholarly-curated attribution and source identification; not independent corroboration of Dio.
references.limits: Do not treat Posen's interpretive overview as another primary witness.

episodes.conflictsAndGeography: The exact extent and violence are disputed and the narrative is Roman and rhetorically charged. No coordinates/individual refuge sites supported. Do not attach Dio's casualty figures to a playable local map.

episodes.date: 115-117 CE; Egyptian local reconstruction is not itself sourced to Alexandria in the cited passage
episodes.place: Alexandria selected, but Dio 68.32 says 'in Egypt' and does not name Alexandria here
episodes.selectedClaim: Diaspora revolts affected Cyrenaica, Egypt and Cyprus during Trajan's war.

references.directlyConsulted: Read the text at lines 153-154; Dio says revolt also occurred in Egypt and Cyprus under Artemion, after describing Cyrene.
references.supports: A revolt in Egypt as a region during these events.
references.limits: This text does not identify Alexandria as the site or provide a harbor episode. Need independent Egyptian papyrus/inscription/archaeological or ancient source for Alexandria-specific local action; the campaign's local reconstruction must be labeled as such.

episodes.conflictsAndGeography: Do not turn 'Egypt' into Alexandria without a separate source. Dio's casualty and atrocity claims are not reliable quantitative evidence; no port geography/event footprint supplied here.

episodes.date: c.130-132 CE; date/order of Hadrian's visit, colony foundation, and revolt is disputed
episodes.place: Jerusalem, renamed Aelia Capitolina in Dio's narrative; no exact founding day/site work evidenced
episodes.selectedClaim: Hadrian visited Judea and promoted a Roman colony at Jerusalem, according to a historical narrative; direct causal link to revolt contested.

references.reference: Cassius Dio, Roman History 69.12.1-3, English translation excerpt by E. Cary
references.directlyConsulted: Read lines 15-18: Dio states Aelia Capitolina was founded at Jerusalem, a Jupiter temple was established at the site of the Jewish temple, and narratively links this to revolt; he describes fortified/refuge positions.
references.supports: Dio's account of Hadrian's Jerusalem colony and the revolt, with his causal framing explicitly attributed to Dio.
references.limits: Dio wrote retrospectively; the quoted passage cannot alone settle chronology or causation. The route says 69.12-14 but only 69.12.1-3 directly read for this audit. No direct primary inscription/civic coin dated to the precise founding moment checked here.

episodes.conflictsAndGeography: Keep date band qualified. Avoid unqualified claim that one act immediately caused the revolt. The text's exact sequencing is Dio's interpretation and does not give a local architectural blueprint.

imageCandidates.author: Daniel Ventura
imageCandidates.limitations: Depicts a scholarly model of pre-destruction Second Temple Jerusalem, not Aelia Capitolina or Hadrianic city fabric; unsuitable as direct visual reference for this episode except explicitly labeled inherited topography.

episodes.date: 132-135 CE (common reference chronology; some accounts use 132-136)
episodes.place: Judaean Desert refuge caves and regional revolt areas; no single generalized 'Judean Hills' location for all objects
episodes.selectedClaim: Bar Kokhba revolt against Rome; rebel coinage and desert documents attest administration.

references.reference: Israel Antiquities Authority / Shrine of the Book, 'Bar Kokhba Revolt Refuge Caves', sections Wadi Murabba'at and Nahal Hever, lines 82-101
references.directlyConsulted: Read institutional discovery-site descriptions: Wadi Murabba'at has documents mostly dated 132-135, administrative papyri and letters of Shim'on bar Kosiba; Nahal Hever excavations 1960-61 yielded personal documents, military communications and biblical compositions, including a dated cave archive with letters and financial records.
references.supports: Primary papyri/letters and refuge-cave archives provide evidence for administrative and military communications during the revolt period; source names Shim'on bar Kosiba as the official name in documents.
references.limits: Institutional overview, not item catalog/transcription. It does not establish that every object in the caves is rebel administration or a mint record. Nahal Hever Cave of Letters includes dated items from 94-132 CE, so cave assemblages span pre-revolt material as well. Need item-level records before naming specific document, amount, or scene.

references.reference: Israel Museum, Shrine of the Book, overview cited by episode
references.directlyConsulted: Museum page request returned an internal error in this web pass; the claim was cross-checked against the Israel Antiquities Authority/Shrine of the Book discovery-sites page above. Museum page not independently re-read.
references.supports: Not independently assessed from this exact URL here.
references.limits: Do not claim the cited museum page itself was accessed.

references.directlyConsulted: Read Dio 69.12.1-3 at lines 15-18; not all of 69.12-14 in this pass.
references.supports: Roman literary narrative of revolt, fortified refuges and conflict; source attributes cause to colony/temple changes.
references.limits: Retrospective Roman narrative with large-scale claims; not a substitute for papyri/coins and not an independent item catalog.

episodes.conflictsAndGeography: Do not infer one document proves a local mission event. Cave-find provenance matters; distinction among Murabba'at, Nahal Hever and other desert sites must be preserved. The official name in documents is Shim'on ben Kosiba; Bar Kokhba is a later/interpretive epithet, not a neutral contemporaneous personal name.
